Channel example: "Move Over Private Equity. Private Infrastructure Investing: AI Boom Beneficiary? feat. Mike Dorrell" (Stonepeak, about $80B AUM). "49. Project Finance 101 & Infrastructure Investing Basics."

Counterpoint: - "Private operators will do a better job every single time" is a fundraiser's line. Thames Water is the standard counterexample: privatized, over-levered, under-invested. - The "70% of internet traffic goes through Northern Virginia" figure is a widely repeated but unsupported statistic. Treat it as "largest data-center market," nothing more precise. - His claim that finance-trained investors beat operators at investment decisions is candid but self-serving.

Links: canon helmer 7 powers (cornered resource and barriers), canon klarman margin of safety (the "get our money back" test), canon porter competitive strategy.

13. Home-equity investments (HEIs): selling a slice of your house

What it is: A homeowner sells a percentage of the home's equity to an investor for an upfront cash payment, with no monthly payments and no interest. They settle when the home is sold or refinanced, or at term (typically 3-5 years in Findley's framing).

How it works: - Findley's example. - Bought in 2020 for $800k with a $600k mortgage at about 3%. The house is now worth about $1M. - The originator haircuts the value 25% for local price volatility: $750k − $600k = $150k of "adjusted" equity. - It pays $50k for one-third of the equity. - Sell tomorrow and you owe ($1M − $600k)/3 = $133k. - Later, you owe a third of whatever the equity turns out to be, so the originator shares the downside too. It lost money on San Francisco condos during COVID. - Why borrowers use it: - A HELOC requires roughly a 750-780 FICO, and is hard to get for 1099/K-1 earners and investors. - Refinancing means giving up a 2-3% mortgage for 6-plus%. - Findley pitches it as credit-curing: pay off about $50k of credit cards at 18-26%, rebuild the FICO, graduate to a HELOC. - Market context (Jen's Fed and ICE data): household debt $18.8T (Q1 2026, +$4.6T since 2019), credit cards $1.25T, and $17.8T of home equity of which $11.6T is "tappable." - Returns and pipeline: about 17% average returns since 2015 (Bloomberg, via Jen). Tacora buys from originator Point (a16z- and WestCap-backed), which is licensed state by state in ~40 states. Not in Texas, which limits corporations on title.

Business significance / value: It turns illiquid, locked-in home equity into cash without debt service. The investor buys diversified, housing-linked, long-duration equity with no coupon, an asset "without a natural buyer." That is Tacora's role: asset-based capital for venture-backed originators. Tacora grew from a $350M fund I (2022) to $700M at fund II's hard cap, about $1.5-1.6B in total.

Forces & impact: The mortgage lock-in effect (2-3% legacy rates versus about 6.4% today), the K-shaped consumer (wages up 2-3% in real terms while housing, cars, insurance and groceries are up 60-80%), tight post-GFC credit standards, and a housing undersupply that should support prices for 5-10 years.

With vs. without: Without HEIs, a house-rich, cash-poor owner can only sell, refinance at a high rate, or borrow on cards. With them, liquidity comes at the price of giving up upside, with the investor absorbing some downside.

Applies when / Breaks when: Works with rising or stable local prices and a borrower who would otherwise pay 20%-plus. It breaks in a 2008-style national decline (Findley concedes this) and for borrowers who misunderstand the cost.

Channel example: "Hedge Funds Want the Equity in Your Home, feat. Tacora Capital Founder Keri Findley."

Counterpoint (the most important one in this note): Run Findley's own numbers. Settling immediately turns $50k into $133k for the investor, about 2.7x on day one, because the 25% haircut is a discount the homeowner pays up front. Flat prices over 5 years still leave the owner owing at least $133k. A $50k loan at about 9% for 5 years costs roughly $77k in total. Real contracts include caps that limit this, but the product's "no payments" framing hides a high implied cost of capital. The haircut is also the investor's margin of safety: the home can fall 25% before the investor loses a dollar. The ~17% investor return is the homeowner's cost. The hosts, both CDO alumnae, didn't press the point.

Links: canon klarman margin of safety (the haircut as margin of safety), unit 10 personal finance operating system (debt versus equity for a household).

14. Entrepreneurship through acquisition (ETA) and search funds

What it is: Becoming a CEO by buying an existing profitable small business rather than founding one. There are two main models: the search fund (investors pay you to search, then fund the deal) and the self-funded search (your own savings, raising only once you find the deal).

How it works (Jesse Sapphire): - Search-fund economics. Search capital converts into deal equity with a step-up. The searcher holds no common equity up front but receives about 25% of the gain above purchase price plus a hurdle. That's a carry-like option, which suits fast growers (home-health staffing, SaaS) and argues for the biggest deal you can run. It fits poorly with slow, single-digit businesses whose equity is built mostly by paying down debt. Typical real-world structures vest that roughly 25% in tranches: at acquisition, over time, and on IRR hurdles. - Self-funded. You own the equity outright (Sapphire owns 100%). So target a "cockroach": single-digit growth, a long profitable record (ABG has operated since 1992 and survived 9/11 and the GFC), an explainable business, and a sector where you're the ideal customer. - Size bands (rough): - SDE (seller's discretionary earnings, which adds back the owner's pay) of $0-1M: main-street buyers. - About $0.5-3.5M EBITDA: self-funded searchers. ABG was about $1.3-1.5M. His search box was $0.75-2.5M. - Larger: search funds. - About $5-20M EBITDA: LMM PE. - Sourcing. Brokers take about 10% of price. Sapphire mailed a brochure to roughly 250 brokers. One called 18 months later, and the deal fell apart twice in a two-year process. You're "the worst kind of buyer": little money, not strategic, no industry experience, risky to lend to. - Debt stack (example: $10M price): - About $6M bank or SBA debt. SBA loans run 10 years; anyone owning more than 20% must personally guarantee, which rules SBA out for funded search. - About $2M equity. - About $2M seller note: second lien, sometimes on standby, sometimes forgivable instead of an earnout. Banks treat it almost as equity because it keeps the old owner invested in the transition. - Classic trade-off: price or liquidity. A seller who wants top dollar finances part of it. - These are "airball" loans against cash flow with no hard collateral. His borrowing rate is 11.5%. - Asset deal versus stock deal. In an asset deal the buyer leaves past liabilities behind and gets a stepped-up tax basis. He used a 338(h)(10) election: legally a stock deal, taxed as an asset deal.

Business significance / value: The seller (often around 75 years old, without a successor) gets liquidity and legacy. Many sell to "the next version of them" rather than to PE. The buyer gets revenue, profit and staff from day one. Sapphire's short puts the comparison plainly: starting a company takes irrational exuberance, while buying one means revenue, profit and good people on day one. Sapphire argues W-2 careers carry under-appreciated risk. He lost five CEOs and the clients he printed for included Signature, SVB and Credit Suisse.

Forces & impact: The boomer business-succession wave, interest rates (debt service on an 11.5% airball), and SBA program rules. Time horizon turns out to be decisive. In COVID, ABG's revenue fell 95% and staff went from 24 to 4. A 3-5-year search-fund clock would have shut it in April 2020. Permanent capital, PPP and a fully drawn revolver kept it alive. 2024 revenue beat 2019.

With vs. without: Without ETA, many founder-owned firms close or sell to consolidators when the owner retires. When it breaks, the buyer over- "strategizes." Sapphire tells the story of a snowplow-company buyer whose real problem was afternoon Wi-Fi dropping a third of orders. Or the deal dies on hidden concentration, such as five "separate" top clients all referred by one person who golfs with the owner.

Applies when / Breaks when: Works with patient capital, humility ("you are the only thing that changed"), and diligence into concentrations. Breaks with leverage plus a shock under a forced-exit timeline.

Channel example: "Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition 101" (Jesse Sapphire, ABG Print).

Counterpoint: One survivor's story. His "75% of searchers find a deal" is above the Stanford search-fund study's roughly 60-65%. The 25% carry-like structure he described (he didn't take that route) simplifies the tranche vesting. Repo baseline: tiger sisters wealth mechanics claims about 60% of small-business sales include seller financing. This note adds why banks want the seller note and where SBA's guarantee rule bites.

Links: tiger sisters wealth mechanics, entrepreneurship operator playbook, canon akerlof market for lemons (seller information advantage, reps and warranties).

14b. Venture capital from the outside in: fund math, the founder's terms, and when not to raise

What it is: VC is equity for young, unproven companies, raised from LPs into a fund that must return multiples of itself. This section covers what the channel adds from two outside views: the LP's (how the fund math constrains every check) and the founder's (what taking the money commits you to). The firm-level view of seed funds is in primary venture partners insights, harlem capital vc insights and apply wss to venture.

How it works: - Angel versus fund (Camilo Acosta, VC 101, Sept 2023). - An angel's $25k check only has to come back 2-3x. - A $100M fund has to return $300-500M to be good, so each winner must be enormous. Camilo: it's "much easier to make money as an angel." - The LP ladder runs from high-net-worth individuals and family offices to funds of funds, then endowments, foundations and pensions. - Stages keep moving. - Pre-seed: idea, team, maybe an MVP. - Seed: product in market, roughly $10k MRR, under $1M ARR. - Series A at $1-2M ARR. A story alone no longer raises an A. - B onward are growth rounds judged on unit economics and a path to a $5-10B company. - Crossover funds (Tiger, Coatue) pushed down into the A, blurring late VC into growth equity. - Fees and carry. - 2 and 20 is the norm. First-time funds often charge 2.5%, and Sequoia and Founders Fund-tier firms 3 and 30. - Carry arithmetic (his example, my completion): a $20M fund grows to $100M, profit $80M, GP carry $16M, LPs $64M plus their $20M back. - Carry is paid only on realization, which is why skill takes about a decade to judge. - The GP commit is ~1% of the fund, sometimes "cashless": management fees are waived and diverted into the commitment. - The firm usually sits in three entities: the LP fund, the management company and the general partner. - Returns are bimodal. VC is "the highest returning asset class" only in its top quartile. Camilo says the average fund returns about 1x, and he expects many firms to be wiped out. UTIMCO's $129M across Union Square Ventures funds returned $1.18B, about 9.1x (my arithmetic). - SAFEs and pre/post-money. A SAFE (Y Combinator) is a right to future equity that converts at the first priced round. Camilo calls it an interest-free note, which is wrong: it is not debt. A "$2M on $10M" raise matters by definition: - $10M pre-money means a $12M post, so the investor owns 16.7%. - $10M post-money means the investor owns 20%. His fund targets 5% ownership at entry. A Series A lead wants 10-20%. - Liquidation preference (FareHarbor founder, "Mark Cuban told him not to take VC"). Teach it correctly, because the guest's version was wrong: - 1x non-participating. $50k for 0.5% at $10M. On a $20M sale the investor takes the greater of $50k back or 0.5% × $20M = $100k, so $100k, 2x. On a $4M sale it takes $50k back if the preference stack fits under the price, versus $20k pro rata. - Participating. The investor takes $50k and then $100k, $150k in all. That "double dip" is what the guest described as normal. It isn't standard in modern VC. - His practical rule is sound: before writing a check, get in writing whether the valuation is pre or post, what percentage the money buys, what you receive at a $100M exit, and the preference terms. - Why not raise (FareHarbor: booking software for tour operators, sold to Booking Holdings). - About 300 staff and $30-50M of revenue in three years, funded by $5M of venture debt with an equity kicker to buy a competitor. No VC equity. - About to raise $100M, they met Mark Cuban, who called it "vulture capital" and said to take it only if you have a "slot machine": a known CAC and LTV where $100M in reliably becomes $200M out. - The founder's arithmetic: with $100M of preferred on top, a $250M sale stops working for the investors. You need $1B or more, and to get there you hire 700 people, add legal and HR, and lose the lean "local maximum" when profit peaks and an acquirer pays most. - They sold for about $250M a year later. The episode title says $300M; the guest says $250M, matching public reports. - Angel discipline (same guest). - Open with "not investing right now, but I'd love to look," which protects the friendship. - Invest only when founders have put in their own money and sold something. - Distinguish a good business from a good investment: an investment needs a buyer and a timeline. - Prefer bottom-up evidence (1,000 units sold out from one influencer post) to "0.5% of a $1B market." He garbled that as $50M; it is $5M.

Business significance / value: - VC turns founder risk into a portfolio bet in which a few winners pay for everything. The fund captures value through ownership in the winners. - Late entrants capture less. Damodaran's Instacart chart, which Kristen cites, showed returns falling round by round, with the last rounds negative. - For founders, VC buys speed at the price of a higher exit bar and loss of control. Board seats usually arrive at the Series A.

Forces & impact: - Rates: "TINA" became "TARA" (there are reasonable alternatives) at 5.5-6% risk-free, so LPs demand more of risky funds. - The 2022 denominator effect (concept 6). - Exits stuck behind private giants such as Stripe, so funds run to year 12 and beyond (one cited in year 17). - AI: "wrapper" startups have no moat and turn capital-intensive. Camilo prefers the infrastructure layer: "we're still in the 80s and 90s of AI."

With vs. without: Without VC, companies with expensive, uncertain paths (deep tech, network effects) don't get built, and founders grow on debt and cash flow as FareHarbor did. With it, the preference stack and fund math decide which exits count as success. A $250M sale can be a triumph for a bootstrapped founder and a failure for a $100M fund.

Applies when / Breaks when: VC fits when growth really converts capital into durable value at scale (the slot machine) and the outcome can be large enough to return a fund. It breaks when the company is a good business with a natural $250M exit, or when a crowded market lets "anyone with a pulse" raise a fund.

Channel example: "27. Venture Capital 101" (Camilo Acosta). "He Sold His Business for $300mm. Why Mark Cuban Told Him Not to Take Venture Capital."

Counterpoint: - Both guests talk their book: an emerging AI pre-seed manager raising money ("former founders make the best VCs"), and a bootstrapped survivor ("vulture capital"). The second is survivorship: the companies that needed VC and died without it aren't on the show. - Camilo dates and figures several facts loosely. Thiel's Facebook check was at about a $5M valuation, not $2.5M. Sequoia had already split off its China and India arms before the recording. VC fund commitments aren't "redeemed"; LPs stop re-upping or sell in secondaries. - The angel guest's "up to 10%" of wealth in angel deals is aggressive by most planners' norms, and Kristen pushed back.

Links: harlem capital vc insights (waterfall, DPI, J-curve), primary venture partners insights (fund size → ownership → return the fund), apply wss to venture (the WSS layer applied to two seed firms), canon ries lean startup, canon mauboussin success equation (power laws and luck).

15. Sports franchises: league design, scarcity, and arena control

What it is: Major-league teams priced as un-replicable franchises. Each league is a cartel that fixes the number of teams, pools some revenue and may cap costs. That design decides whether a team behaves like an annuity or an option.

How it works: - Revenue mix plus a cost cap is the whole model (the hosts' Sports Investing 101). Split revenue into national (shared media, divided equally) and local (tickets, local TV, sponsorship, arena), then ask whether payroll is capped:

League National / local Payroll Consequence
NFL ~80 / 20 Hard cap (~$255M in 2024, ~$279M in 2025) Small and big markets converge; a half-empty stadium "almost doesn't matter"
NBA ~60 / 40 Soft cap: luxury tax plus first and second "aprons" Overspending is punished; playoff runs add revenue each round
MLB ~20 / 80 No cap Market size rules: Soto's $765M/15-year Mets deal; "maybe six of 30" teams make real money
  • The NFL TV arithmetic. $110B over 11 years is $10B a year, or ~$312M per team. Kristen's "~$400M a year" per team is closer to total national revenue.
  • The NBA tax. The 2024-25 aprons were ~$178M and ~$189M. The hosts illustrated a single "4.2x" penalty on dollars over the second apron. The real tax is bracketed from the tax line, steps up every $5M, and is steeper for repeat offenders. The aprons mainly bite as roster-building restrictions.
  • Comps:
  • Lakers: $10B for a majority stake (2025).
  • Celtics: about $6.1B, structured as 51% now and the rest in 2028.
  • Washington Commanders: $6B (2023).
  • Denver Broncos: $4.7B (2022).
  • Mets: Steve Cohen paid $2.4B for 95% in 2020.
  • Who may own a team. Historically an NFL team needed one billionaire paying cash (David Tepper, Panthers). In 2024 the NFL approved a list of PE funds for minority stakes: Arctos, Ares, Sixth Street, and a consortium including Blackstone and Carlyle. Per public reports, the cap is 10% per fund per team, with a minimum hold. Sixth Street then bought into the Patriots and Celtics, built Bay FC (NWSL) from rights to the field in 14 months, and financed Real Madrid's stadium renovation against future stadium revenue rights. Leagues police conflicts too: Michael Rubin had to sell his Sixers stake when Fanatics entered sports betting, and Adelman bought it to become the third-largest partner in HBSE.
  • The trickle-down (hosts). Family offices shut out of the big funds chase "micro-sports" (smaller leagues, women's teams, adjacencies). Eli Manning's Brand Velocity Group invests around teams (media, equipment, collectibles, gaming) rather than in them.
  • Arena control is a second asset (Adelman).
  • The Sixers rent from the Flyers and Comcast, so they miss building revenue and don't control the fan experience.
  • The new ~$1.5B South Philadelphia arena (opening 2030, or 2031 in the earlier clip) is a 50/50 partnership. Retail, food and the district's apartments and hotel feed the team's value: team and arena are "hand and glove."
  • HBSE's Prudential Center in Newark runs 240+ events a year with one pro tenant.
  • When a tenant team's lease expires, either the landlord makes "a great offer to stay" or the team must raise $1.5B for its own building.
  • The Premier League contrast (Crystal Palace). No salary cap. Rivals include sovereign wealth funds that can spend $300M on one player. Relegation drops the bottom three clubs a division, and revenue collapses. Adelman said "bottom two"; it is three. The realistic owner goal is "keep me in the middle of the pack."

Business significance / value: - US closed leagues with pooled national media and caps turn teams into contracted, monopoly-like media annuities, structurally close to infrastructure (concept 12). - Sellers capture the scarcity premium. The league protects it by limiting supply ("It's 30 teams. That's it," Adelman). Owners who control the arena capture building revenue; tenants don't. - Open, relegation-based leagues add binary downside and an arms race against state money.

Forces & impact: - Media-rights inflation. The NBA's new deal is ~$76B over 11 years; the hosts said 10. - Leagues admitting institutional capital, which widens the buyer pool and lifts every owner's mark. - Billionaires and sovereign funds set the marginal price. - Second-order: each record sale re-marks every other team. Adelman doesn't think any NBA owner was upset by the Celtics price. Comps set by hometown-pride buyers become everyone's valuation, which is circular.

With vs. without: Without closed leagues, teams behave like Premier League clubs: high variance, owners as patrons, frequent losses. With them, trophy pricing keeps setting records, and the risk shifts to whether media rights keep compounding.

Applies when / Breaks when: Works while national media rights keep growing and leagues keep supply fixed. It would break if streaming-era rights stopped escalating, or in MLB-style leagues where local revenue and no cap let a few rich markets outspend the rest.

Channel example: "Sports Investing Basics & Interview with Eli Manning and David Adelman." "Co-Owner of Philly 76ers David Adelman on Sports Investing, Real Estate and Early Stage Investing." "PE | Growth Equity Value Creation w Sixth Street's Paul Dodd" (Bay FC, Real Madrid). "Real Estate PE 101" (intro segment). "Why Owning a Soccer Team in the Premier League is WILD" (short).

Counterpoint: - Adelman's "scarcity justifies the price" is the view of an owner whose stake is re-marked by every record sale. - Kristen's claim that the Giants and Chiefs are worth "roughly the same" overstates the NFL's parity. A high national share narrows the gap between markets; it doesn't erase it. - The Packers are not "publicly traded": their shares can't be transferred and pay no dividends. - MLB's national media income is roughly $1.5-2B a year, not the "$1B" the hosts said. - The Millennium aside from the same Real Estate PE intro still stands as illustrative only: ~12x "operating cash flow" ($14B / $1.125B) versus 4-6x for hedge funds and 15-20x for PE managers. Its fee math slips: 20% × 20% × $75B is $3B, not "$2-2.25B." - The Lakers deal structure is in wss credit distressed.

Links: canon helmer 7 powers (scarcity as cornered resource), wss credit distressed (Lakers financing), unit 09 capital light businesses (the league office as asset-light franchisor).

How the concepts connect

ZIRP 2019-21 ─► record LP commitments + high entry multiples + cheap layered debt (7) ─► "anyone with a pulse" raises a VC fund (14b)
     │                                   │
     ▼                                   ▼
NAV swells, marks optimistic (6)    sub lines flatter early IRR (3)
     │
rates ↑ ─► leverage is no longer an edge ─► returns must come from EBITDA: operating partners, AI in go-to-market (2b)
     │
     ├─► exits stall ─► distributions/NAV at GFC low (6) ─► LPs can't recommit ─► fundraising slows
     │        │
     │        └─► public drawdown (Apr 2025) + endowment tax ─► denominator effect ─► Yale sells ~$6B LP-led (6)
     │
     ├─► liquidity engineering: LP-led & GP-led secondaries (5) ─► CVs re-fee winners (tiered carry), sub lines + deferred payments,
     │   NAV loans, CFOs, div recaps (7)
     │
     └─► new LP needed ─► wealth channel (9) ─► advisor choice: wirehouse shelf vs RIA (9b) ─► evergreen wrappers (8)
                                               │                                           ─► best-fit assets = secondaries (5) & co-invest (4)
                     constant inflows ─► deployment pressure ─► entry prices ↑ ─► future returns ↓ (2)
                     quarterly marks ─► "volatility laundering" ─► gates if redemptions > 5%/qtr
                     401(k) executive order ─► the largest pool yet, sold in 5-minute advisor pitches (8, 9)

Same rate shock in real assets: cap rates ↑ ─► negative leverage ─► CRE refi gap (11) ─► pref/mezz rescue capital
                                 and households: 2% → 7% mortgage lock-in ─► home-equity investments (13)
Duration as the antidote: infrastructure and project finance (12), permanent-capital ETA (14), closed-league franchises (15)
Scarcity as the antidote: fixed league supply + pooled media + caps ─► record comps ─► PE whitelisted into the NFL (15)

The single idea underneath: private markets trade liquidity and price transparency for control and an illiquidity premium. Every product in this note is a way to re-sell some liquidity (secondaries, evergreens, HEIs), borrow against illiquidity (sub lines, NAV loans), or exploit someone else's need for it (gap capital, distressed debt).

Retrieval questions

  1. A fund shows 35% IRR and 1.15x TVPI in year two. What two questions do you ask? How much was funded on a subscription line before capital was called, and what DPI does it have? Early IRR is timing-sensitive and can be manufactured. The multiple and cash distributed are not.
  2. Why can distributions hit a record and still be at a GFC-low as a share of NAV? The denominator (unrealized NAV) ballooned from 2018-21 inflows and optimistic marks. In 2008, by contrast, the numerator went to zero.
  3. An evergreen fund charges 1.25% and 12.5% over a 5% hurdle. A drawdown fund charges 1.5% and 20% over 8%. Why might the evergreen cost more? Its carry crystallizes every year on unrealized gains, over a lower hurdle. Drawdown carry waits until capital and pref are returned, often in years 4-6.
  4. Why are secondaries the natural core of semi-liquid funds? They're already invested (no blind-pool cash drag), diversified at once, and mature enough to distribute cash for redemptions.
  5. Shah wants her LMM GPs to earn carry. Why is that an alignment argument, not a generosity one? Carry requires selling, which produces distributions. Fee income from ever-larger funds rewards asset gathering instead.
  6. An office building quotes a 6 cap. Why might an investor's true yield be closer to 4? Recurring tenant buildouts and leasing commissions are capital spent below the NOI line every time leases roll.
  7. Why did infrastructure investing start in Australia, not the US? Australian states privatized assets in the 1990s and Macquarie raised listed retail capital to bid. US public owners already had cheap, tax-exempt muni financing (6% taxable ≈ 4% muni).
  8. Same 15% annual return: why does Dorrell prize it over 20 years far more than over 5? Compounding. 2.0x versus about 16.4x. Duration, not the rate, is infrastructure's edge.
  9. Using Findley's numbers, what does a homeowner who sells immediately pay for $50k of HEI cash? $133k, about 2.7x. The 25% volatility haircut is a discount transferred to the investor up front and doubles as the investor's margin of safety.
  10. Why can't a classic search-fund deal use SBA debt? SBA requires a personal guarantee from anyone holding more than 20% of the equity, which search-fund investors won't give.
  11. Why did First Brands put Apollo on its disqualified-lender list? Apollo's Caesars-era reputation for aggressive restructuring tactics, and its ownership of competitor Tenneco, which would have given it data room access.
  12. What makes an infrastructure asset different from Walmart, in Dorrell's framing? Mismanagement doesn't kill it, because nobody can build a competing airport or utility. That earns cheap financing and lower returns, and invites regulation.
  13. Blackstone shows a private-markets portfolio beating 60/40 by 1 point a year with 1.8 points less volatility (2016-24). Name three reasons an individual investor wouldn't capture that. Fees (the indices are largely gross), appraisal smoothing (the volatility gap is partly measurement), and mismatched return types (pooled IRRs against time-weighted returns). Bonus: a short, low-rate window, and redemption gates that the backtest never had to face.
  14. A GP moves a 4x winner into a continuation vehicle at 400 and charges 75 bps instead of 2%. Why is the GP still better off than selling? It crystallizes carry on the old fund at 400, rolls that carry into the CV to keep compounding, and earns new tiered carry (10/15/20 over rising IRR and MOIC hurdles). 75 bps on 400 is 3, more than 2% on the original 100.
  15. Why do 80-99% of LPs choosing to sell in a CV not prove the deal was fair to them? A high sell rate mostly shows the price was full relative to NAV. The test of fairness is the third-party auction plus the GP rolling all its economics. And the sponsor's own advisor ran the process.
  16. Public equities drop 25% and private marks barely move. Walk through why a long-horizon endowment might sell PE stakes anyway. Private becomes overweight against target (the denominator effect), distributions have stalled so no cash is coming in, and new commitments to core GPs still need funding. Selling on the secondary market at strong prices rebalances and recycles. Yale's ~$6B sale is the case.
  17. Why can Harvard absorb a $2B funding cut that would break a $230M endowment, beyond the obvious size difference? Endowments spend from returns and much of the money is donor-restricted. A small endowment can't earn much without risking principal, so it runs conservatively and earns less. Size buys both buffer and return.
  18. A big bank quotes a lower advisory fee than an RIA. What's the first question? Who else pays the bank? Shelf-space revenue sharing from product managers and lending economics can subsidize the quoted fee (Moffett).
  19. In Kristen's returns bridge, why is operating improvement worth more than its EBITDA effect alone? Higher EBITDA raises exit EV at a constant multiple and produces cash that pays down debt, moving value from lenders to equity. It may also earn a higher multiple at exit. Leverage alone stopped being an edge once everyone could borrow cheaply.
  20. $2M on a "$10M" SAFE: what's the investor's ownership if $10M is pre-money, and if it's post-money? 16.7% ($2M of $12M) versus 20% ($2M of $10M).
  21. A founder takes $100M of VC and later gets a $250M offer. Why might the deal no longer work? The fund needs a multiple on $100M of preferred, so a $250M exit barely returns the preference and fails the fund math. The company now has to chase $1B+, which changes hiring, burn and risk. That was Cuban's "slot machine" test.
  22. Why does an NFL team in Kansas City trade at a value closer to a New York team than an MLB team in a small market does to the Yankees? About 80% of NFL revenue is pooled national media split equally, under a hard cap. MLB is about 80% local with no cap, so market size drives revenue and payroll.
  23. Why did the Sixers' new arena deal matter for team valuation? As a tenant they missed building revenue and control of the fan experience. As a 50/50 owner they share retail, food and district income, and a buyer of the team gets both.
